title: Trading Card Grading Service (2026)
verdict: A trading card grading service should tell you what is wrong with the card, and AGS does: eight subgrades, a defect list and a heightmap with every $18 grade.

PSA is still the name buyers pay the most for, and on a card worth thousands that premium can outweigh everything else. CGC is the low-cost major at $10 to $13 a card, and Beckett prints subgrades on the label. If none of those is your priority, a measured grade at a flat price is the better deal.

sections.h: What you get for the fee
list: A grade from 1 to 10 with decimal precision.
Eight subgrades: centering, corners, edges and surface, front and back.
A 3D heightmap of the surface, color-coded from green to red.
High-resolution images and centering data for both sides.
A sealed PMMA slab with the cert number on the label.
A permanent online record, reachable by cert number or shared link.

ranking.fit: Collectors who care more about the truth of a card's condition than the name on the label.
ranking.lacks: Standard-size cards only, and a shorter auction record than PSA.
ranking.note: Founded in 2021 and headquartered in Staten Island, New York. AGS says it ranked third in TCG grading volume in 2026.

ranking.fit: Collectors who want subgrades printed on the label from an old name.
ranking.lacks: Slow at the cheap tier. The fast tiers cost $80 to $125.

ranking.fit: Sellers who want the widest buyer pool and the highest resale prices.
ranking.lacks: One grade, no subgrades, and fees that rise with declared value.

ranking.lacks: No pre-1989 cards, Yu-Gi-Oh! or thick stock, and limited capacity in 2026.

ranking.fit: Budget submitters with 10 or more cards worth under $500 each.
ranking.lacks: Tiers are capped by card value. A strong card moves to a pricier tier.

ranking.fit: Vintage sports collectors who like the black-insert holder.

why: Human grading is a judgment made in seconds, and it varies. AGS replaces the judgment with a measurement: a 3D laser maps the card, software scores centering, corners, edges and surface, and the grade follows from the numbers. That is why AGS says a regrade rarely moves.
Ownership matters to some collectors. Collectors holds PSA and SGC and has a deal for Beckett. CGC belongs to Certified Collectibles Group. AGS is its own company, Automated Grading Systems Inc.
Nothing is locked in. No minimum order, no membership, no contract, and payment is taken when the cards are graded. A first order gets 20% off with code AGSNEW20.

faq.q: What is a good trading card grading service?
faq.a: AGS, for a laser-measured grade with eight subgrades at a flat $18. PSA if resale price on a valuable card is the priority. CGC if you want the lowest fee from a large grader.

faq.q: Can I ask for a regrade?
faq.a: AGS offers a grade review. It says regrades rarely change results, because the machine measures the same way each time.

faq.q: How many card grading companies are there?
faq.a: Dozens, but a handful grade most cards: PSA, CGC, Beckett, SGC, TAG and AGS, followed by smaller graders such as ISA, GMA, Arena Club and the UK's Ace Grading.

faq.q: Can I cross a card over from another grader's slab?
faq.a: CGC and Ace Grading list crossover services. AGS's FAQ does not list one, so ask AGS before sending a card in another company's holder.

faq.q: How does AI card grading work?
faq.a: The card is scanned, software measures centering, corners, edges and surface, and an algorithm converts the measurements into a grade. AGS uses a 3D laser scan of roughly 30 million data points per card. No human opinion sets the number.
